title: Catalyst Comet: Hetero and Homogeneous
welcome_lead: Compare heterogeneous and homogeneous TM catalysis.
meta_desc: A-Level chemistry adventure on transition metal catalysis.
final_note: You watched catalysts cycle through oxidation states.

concepts.def: Catalyst in different phase to reactants.

walkthroughs.body_html:
Fe in Haber (N2 + 3H2 -> 2NH3). V2O5 in Contact (SO2 + 1/2 O2 -> SO3). Ni in alkene hydrogenation.

Pt/Pd/Rh in catalytic converters: 2CO + 2NO -> 2CO2 + N2. Reactants adsorb, react, desorb.

Fe^2+/Fe^3+ catalyses S2O8^2- + 2I- -> 2SO4^2- + I2.

Step 1: S2O8^2- + 2Fe^2+ -> 2SO4^2- + 2Fe^3+. Step 2: 2Fe^3+ + 2I- -> 2Fe^2+ + I2. Net is original equation; Fe regenerated.

5C2O4^2- + 2MnO4- + 16H+ -> 10CO2 + 2Mn^2+ + 8H2O. Mn^2+ product catalyses the reaction.

Rate is initially slow, accelerates as Mn^2+ accumulates, then slows again as reactants run out.

mcqs.q: What distinguishes a heterogeneous from a homogeneous catalyst?
options: Heterogeneous catalysts are consumed; homogeneous catalysts are not.
A heterogeneous catalyst is in a different phase from the reactants; a homogeneous catalyst is in the same phase.
Heterogeneous catalysts are solid and homogeneous catalysts are liquid — full stop.
A catalyst decreases Kc by stabilising the reactants.

mcqs.q: Does adding a catalyst change the value of Kc?
options: A catalyst decreases Kc by stabilising the reactants.
A catalyst increases Kc by favouring product formation.
No — a catalyst speeds up forward and reverse reactions equally, so Kc is unchanged.
Heterogeneous catalysts are consumed; homogeneous catalysts are not.

mcqs.q: Why are most transition metal complex ions coloured?
options: Transition metals are coloured because their nuclei emit photons in the visible range.
Heterogeneous catalysts are consumed; homogeneous catalysts are not.
Ligands split the d-orbitals into two energy levels; electrons absorb visible light to jump between them (d-d transitions), and the complementary colour is transmitted.
Transition metal ions are coloured because they have a half-full d-subshell which naturally absorbs light.
